hints: Focus on what actually controls how many gas particles are present, not the identity of the gas itself.
Since volume is the same at 1.00 dm3 for all four, compare the ratio p divided by T in kelvin, with T = °C + 273.
The smallest p/T value means the smallest moles and therefore the fewest molecules, so check which sample combines low pressure with high temperature.
walkthrough:
**Link molecules to moles**

The number of molecules is directly proportional to the number of moles, n. More moles means more molecules.

Chemical principle:
$$n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$

**Simplify the comparison**

Here V is the same (1.00 dm3) for all samples and R is constant. So n depends only on p divided by T.

Comparison rule:
$$n \propto \frac{p}{T} \text{ where T must be in kelvin}$$

**Convert temperatures to kelvin**

Always add 273 to the Celsius temperature before using gas laws.

$$A: T = 27 + 273 = 300 \text{ K}$$
$$B: T = 100 + 273 = 373 \text{ K}$$
$$C: T = 300 + 273 = 573 \text{ K}$$
$$D: T = 250 + 273 = 523 \text{ K}$$

**Compare p/T and decide**

A larger T lowers n, a larger p raises n. Calculate p/T in kPa K-1:

$$A: \frac{2.0}{300} = 0.00667$$
$$B: \frac{2.0}{373} = 0.00536$$
$$C: \frac{4.0}{573} = 0.00698$$
$$D: \frac{3.0}{523} = 0.00574$$

The smallest value is for the hydrogen sample, so it contains the fewest moles and therefore the fewest molecules.

options.A: This has the same pressure as B but a much lower temperature (300 K). Lower T at the same p and V gives more moles from n = pV/RT, so it contains more molecules, not the fewest.
options.B: This combines the lowest pressure (2.0 kPa) with a relatively high temperature (373 K). Its p/T ratio is the smallest of the four, so n = pV/RT is smallest and it contains the fewest molecules.
options.C: Although temperature is highest (573 K), pressure is doubled to 4.0 kPa. The increase in p outweighs the increase in T, giving the largest p/T ratio and the most molecules. Students who look only at temperature fall for this trap.
options.D: Pressure is higher (3.0 kPa) and temperature is high (523 K). Its p/T ratio is small but still larger than B, so it has slightly more molecules. It is the second fewest, which makes it a tempting distractor.
